hook: Your ad accounts just went dark. What can you still prove you did?

Today, save what's yours to keep:
- Your own performance reviews and kind notes from managers
- Links to work that is already public: live campaigns, landing pages, posts, bylines, webinars
- Your own notes in your own words: the goal, what you owned, what you tested

Leave behind customer lists, internal dashboards and anything marked confidential. Not sure what you may show? Ask HR in writing.

topic: Senior: bridge job vs target role
hook: Bridge job or target role? Let your runway number decide, not your nerves.

Bridge job or target role? Let your runway number decide, not your nerves.

Panic takes the first offer. A plan sets the date by which you'd take one.

The rough test (a test, not a rule):
- Plenty of months: protect the search and be selective.
- Getting short: a bridge job, contract or fractional project can be the right call. Choose it on purpose, and pick one you can leave.
- Very short: cover essentials first. A bridge job is a decision about time, not a verdict on your career.

Two cautions. Treat income as unconfirmed until it's signed. And if you collect unemployment, earnings usually must be reported and rules vary by state, so ask your state agency first.

Many lenders and card companies have hardship or payment-relief programs, but what's offered varies by company, product and state. Ask; don't assume. Waiting until you're behind can add fees and make the conversation harder.

Before the call: have your account number, balance, due date and what you can pay, even if it's less than usual.

Say: 'I was laid off on [date] and my income has changed. I want to stay current. What hardship or payment-relief options do you offer?'

Then ask what each option costs (fees, interest, end date), how it will be reported to the credit bureaus, and for the terms in writing. Note the date, the person's name and a reference number. You don't have to accept the first offer.

The Budget worksheet (page 31) has columns for due date and 'who I called.' The CFPB has guidance on unexpected job loss. General information, not financial or legal advice.

topic: Student loans and a smaller paycheck
hook: Your income dropped. Your student loan payment didn't. Call the servicer before you miss one.
body:
Your income dropped. Your student loan payment didn't. Call the servicer before you miss one.

A missed payment can turn a stressful month into a worse one. Options exist, but you have to ask for them, and they differ by loan type.

First step: find your servicer, the company you send payments to. For federal loans, the official federal student aid site lists them. For private loans, call the lender directly.

Then ask: what repayment, deferment or forbearance options exist for your loan type; what each does to interest and your balance; whether an income-based plan is available and which documents they'd need. Get the answer in writing, with the date.

hook: Search your target job title on LinkedIn. Does your profile look like the first five results?

Search your target job title on LinkedIn. Does your profile look like the first five results?

If your headline says 'Marketing professional | Open to opportunities' and theirs say 'Lifecycle Marketing Manager | Email automation and retention,' a recruiter searching by role and skill is less likely to land on you. Every week it stays that way, your outreach sends people to a profile that doesn't say what you want.

The 10-minute test:
1. Type the exact title you're targeting into the search bar.
2. Open five profiles of people who hold it.
3. Write down the words their headlines and About sections share.
4. Keep only the words that honestly describe you.

Don't copy anyone's wording or claim a skill you don't have. You're matching vocabulary, not borrowing identity.

Day 12 of the plan (page 14) turns this into a headline and About section, and Day 10 (page 12) does the same exercise with job postings.

Your first message in two years shouldn't also be a request.

The research behind our plan (a study of LinkedIn experiments with over 20 million people) found that acquaintances, not close friends, were linked to the most job mobility, up to a point. People you know a little can reach places your circle can't. But going cold and asking for a job in week three makes it hard for anyone to say yes.

Warm them up now, laid off or not. Each week: pick two people you've worked with and lost touch with. Send a short note with nothing to ask for: a thank-you, a link you thought they'd like, congratulations on their news. Keep a list of who and when.

The image is page 16, the Week 3 opener: 'Reach out. People want to help more than you think.' That week starts with Day 15: a list of 30 people and 20 organizations that hire for your target role, plus three if-then plans.

Warm contacts take weeks, and your runway sets how many weeks you have. Count it first: the Budget tab is free, link in the first comment.

The common wrong move after a layoff: message only the five people you feel comfortable with, hear "I'll keep an ear out," and stop. Two weeks later your search is still inside one small circle.

Order your first ten messages like this:
1. Former managers and close coworkers. Warmest, fastest yes.
2. Agency contacts, freelancers and vendor reps you worked with.
3. Weaker ties: classmates, people from marketing communities, a friend of a friend.

Do not decide anyone is "too senior" or "not helpful." Let them decide.

hook: Freelance, contract and fractional are not the same bridge. Pick on purpose.
body:
Freelance, contract and fractional are not the same bridge. Pick on purpose.

Freelance: project-based, and you find your own clients.
Contract: a company hires you for a set period and scope, often close to full time.
Fractional: a few hours a week for one or more companies, usually at a senior level.

The wrong pick costs hours. Freelance can eat your week finding clients instead of searching. Contract can look like a job but end on a date. Fractional can pay less than you expect before it pays more.

Each one changes your taxes, your health coverage, how unemployment treats your earnings and the time left for your search. Rules vary by state and situation, so check official sources and a tax professional before you sign.

Three questions first: How many hours can I give? Can I show this work afterward? Will it block my search?

Write down your answer to the hours question first.

hook: One panic move can cost you thousands after a layoff: cashing out your 401(k).
body:
One panic move can cost you thousands after a layoff: cashing out your 401(k).

Your 401(k) belongs to you. But cashing out early counts as income that year, and under age 59 and a half you often owe an extra 10% tax. A check made out to you has 20% withheld for federal tax, and you must replace that 20% from other money within 60 days to roll over the full amount.

The plan's rule of thumb: withdrawing retirement money should be the last tool, after budget cuts, unemployment and lender hardship programs. Take a week before deciding, and talk to a tax professional first. This is general information, not tax advice.

First step: know how many months you have before you need to touch it. That is the Budget tab, and it is free.

topic: Reference and what you can ask for
hook: Do you know what your old employer will say when a recruiter calls?

Do you know what your old employer will say when a recruiter calls?

If you still have a severance agreement open, ask before you sign. A severance agreement usually asks you to give up the right to sue, and what you give up stays given up.

The severance cheat sheet asks: "What reference or message will the employer give about me?" Many employers expect a counteroffer. Two things you can ask for that people forget: a neutral reference letter and extra time to decide. The page lists more.

One line from the Toolkit's reference email: "Could you confirm what reference or message the company will give to employers who call about me?"

Ask in writing, stay polite and keep a copy. If anything looks unfair or discriminatory, speak to an employment lawyer or the EEOC; deadlines are short. This is not legal advice.

Thank you for following along these thirty days.

If you are a laid-off marketer who read one post or all of them, here is where the plan lands: money and paperwork first, then a resume and LinkedIn aimed at one role, three case studies, outreach and a weekly routine. Day 30 on page 2 is protected, portfolio-ready and reaching out. It does not promise a job, and neither do we.

If you want that structure in files you can use, the Laid-Off Marketer's 30-Day Job Loss Plan is a 36-page book, a Google Sheet tracker (Budget, Job Tracker, Outreach, Weekly Review, Scorecard) and a 12-page Bonus Toolkit.

$24.99, one-time. Book, Google Sheet and Toolkit. 7-day refund.

Not useful in the first 7 days? Message us for a refund. We ask that you stop using the files.

If not, the free pack and these posts are still here.
